lesson.menu_title: I Have Been Painting -- Vermiculite and Beyond
lesson.menu_desc: Talking about your creative process: present perfect continuous (I have been painting for... / lately I have been experimenting... / how long have you been...?) and -ing subjects, plus the words of the studio -- medium, canvas, sketch, pigment, technique, trial and error, creative block, inspiration, body of work, self-taught
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 35 -- Vermiculite and Beyond: I Have Been Painting
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Maria Claudia Curimbaba | Lesson 35 -- Vermiculite and Beyond: I Have Been Painting
lesson.grammar_point: present perfect continuous (I have been painting for... / how long have you been...?) and -ing subjects

listenings.text: People often ask me how I start a painting. The honest answer is that I do not start with a plan. For the last three years, I have been working with materials that most painters avoid: sand, ash, and even coffee. Every material behaves differently. Ash makes the color darker as it dries, and sand cracks if the layer is too thick. So most of my mornings are trial and error. I make a small sketch, I test the mix on a piece of wood, and I wait a day to see what happens. Working this way is slow, and I have thrown away more tests than I can count. But it has taught me something important. When you stop fighting the material, it starts to show you the painting.

For thirty years, I have been running a family construction company, and for the last twelve, I have been painting in the evenings. People think the two have nothing in common. I disagree. Painting has made me a better manager. On a canvas, like in a project, you make a decision, you look at the result, and you change what does not work. I have also learned to live with creative block. Some weeks nothing happens in the studio, and I have stopped worrying about it. Walking, reading or visiting a museum usually brings the inspiration back. My advice is simple. Do not wait until you have time. Twenty minutes a day is enough to keep a body of work alive.

extra_audio.text: First, you make a small sketch of the idea. Then, you test the mix of pigment and vermiculite on a piece of wood. After that, you wait a day to see how the texture dries. Next, you paint the canvas in thin layers, one at a time. Finally, you step back, look at the whole body of work and decide what to change.
